Floating-point numbers occupy a finite number of bits, so most real values cannot be stored exactly. Each arithmetic operation in IEEE 754 computes the exact mathematical result conceptually and then rounds it to the nearest representable value, which means every addition potentially discards information. Because the amount discarded depends on the magnitudes of the two operands involved, the order in which a sum is accumulated changes which bits survive. The classic illustration uses a large value and two tiny ones: if the tiny quantities are added to the large one individually, each may fall entirely below the last bit of the large number's significand and vanish, whereas if the two tiny values are summed together first they may combine into something big enough to alter the final result. Thus (a + b) + c and a + (b + c) can differ, sometimes dramatically when catastrophic cancellation is involved. Addition remains commutative, since rounding does not care which operand came first, but it is not associative, and it does not distribute cleanly over multiplication either.

Matrix multiplication is built from dot products, and a dot product is a reduction, a long chain of additions whose mathematical value is order-independent but whose floating-point value is not. High-performance implementations exploit this freedom aggressively. They split the inner dimension into tiles that fit in cache, accumulate several partial sums in parallel to hide the latency of the floating-point pipeline, use vector registers so that lanes accumulate strided subsets of the terms, distribute slices of the reduction across threads or across GPU warps that combine results through tree-shaped or atomic reductions, and sometimes use fused multiply-add, which rounds once instead of twice. Each of these choices imposes a particular grouping of the summands. Change the number of threads, the tile size, the vector width, the library version, the hardware generation, or the scheduling of atomic operations, and the grouping changes with it, so the computed product changes in its low-order bits even though the inputs and the algorithm are nominally identical.

The practical consequence is that bitwise reproducibility is not guaranteed across machines, thread counts, or even repeated runs when nondeterministic reduction orders are used. The discrepancies are usually tiny relative to the magnitude of the result, but they can be amplified by ill-conditioned problems, by iterative solvers whose branch decisions or convergence tests depend on exact comparisons, or by long training runs in which a difference of one bit diverges into visibly different trajectories. Remedies include fixing the reduction order deterministically, using compensated or higher-precision accumulation, or employing reproducible summation algorithms that pre-split values by exponent so the result is independent of ordering, all of which trade some performance for repeatability.

Floating-point numbers are stored with a fixed number of significand bits, so most results of an arithmetic operation cannot be represented exactly and must be rounded to the nearest representable value. Addition of two floating-point numbers is therefore not the exact mathematical sum but that sum rounded, and rounding is where associativity breaks down. Consider adding a very large number, a very small number, and the negation of the large number. If the large numbers are added first, they cancel exactly and the small number survives; if the large number and the small number are added first, the small one is shifted so far right during alignment of exponents that it falls off the end of the significand and is discarded entirely, after which the cancellation leaves zero. Both orderings are individually correct to within one rounding error of each intermediate step, yet they disagree completely. More generally, each partial sum introduces a rounding error proportional to its own magnitude, so an ordering that lets partial sums grow large accumulates larger absolute errors than one that keeps them small, which is why summing in increasing order of magnitude, or pairwise, or with compensated schemes such as Kahan summation, gives better accuracy than naive left-to-right accumulation. Catastrophic cancellation amplifies this: when a later subtraction removes most of the leading digits, the previously accumulated rounding noise is promoted to a large relative error.

Matrix multiplication is a dense collection of dot products, and a dot product is exactly such a summation. Nothing in a high-performance implementation preserves a single canonical order of accumulation. Blocking and tiling for cache reuse split the reduction dimension into chunks whose partial results are combined at the end; vectorization keeps several independent accumulators in SIMD lanes and merges them afterwards; multithreading and GPU implementations partition the reduction across cores, warps, or entire devices and combine partial sums in a tree whose shape depends on how many workers happened to participate; fused multiply-add eliminates one rounding step in some code paths but not others; and library heuristics select different kernels according to matrix shape, alignment, hardware generation, and even runtime load. Consequently the same mathematical product computed twice can differ in its last bits, and those differences are not merely cosmetic. They propagate and amplify through iterative solvers, training loops, and branch conditions, so two runs may diverge into visibly different outcomes. Reproducibility therefore requires explicit effort: fixing thread counts and kernel selection, using deterministic reduction trees, or paying for higher-precision or compensated accumulation, all of which trade some performance for bit-identical results.

Floating-point numbers represent only a finite subset of the reals: an IEEE 754 double, for instance, carries a 53-bit significand and a separate exponent. The exact sum of two such numbers frequently needs more significand bits than the format provides, so the hardware rounds the result to the nearest representable value before the next operation begins. Each individual addition is deterministic and correctly rounded, but the rounding error it commits depends on the relative magnitudes of its two operands. Change the order in which the same set of numbers is combined and you change which intermediate magnitudes meet each other, and therefore which bits get discarded. The classic illustration is that (1 + 10^16) − 10^16 evaluates to zero, because adding one to 10^16 cannot be represented and rounds back to 10^16, whereas 1 + (10^16 − 10^16) evaluates to one. Absorption of small values by large ones, catastrophic cancellation when nearly equal quantities are subtracted, and edge effects such as intermediate overflow to infinity or gradual underflow into subnormals all mean that addition is commutative but not associative, and not distributive with multiplication either.

Matrix multiplication is essentially a large collection of dot products, and a dot product is a reduction, so it inherits this sensitivity directly. A high-performance implementation almost never sums the K products left to right. It tiles the loops to fit cache, so partial sums are accumulated per block and then combined; it vectorizes, so eight or sixteen SIMD lanes each hold an independent running sum that is folded together at the end; it may fuse multiply and add, eliminating one rounding step entirely; it may split the K dimension across threads or GPU blocks, with partial results merged through atomics or a second pass whose order depends on which worker finishes first; and on tensor cores it may accumulate in a different precision than the inputs. Libraries also switch among several hand-tuned kernels according to matrix shape, alignment, core count, and hardware generation.

Every one of these choices is a different reduction order, and each yields a slightly different, equally legitimate answer. Consequently the same mathematical product can differ in its last bits between two machines, two library versions, two thread counts, or even two runs of the same nondeterministic kernel. The discrepancies are tiny in a relative sense, bounded roughly by the length of the reduction times the machine epsilon times the sum of the magnitudes of the terms, but they are not tiny relative to the result when heavy cancellation occurs, and they can be amplified by iterative solvers, comparisons, ties in an argmax, or the chaotic dynamics of training. Bitwise reproducibility therefore requires deliberately fixing the reduction order, or using wider accumulators or compensated and exactly rounded summation schemes, all of which cost performance.

Floating-point numbers occupy a finite number of bits, so each arithmetic result must be rounded to the nearest representable value. Addition of two doubles is computed exactly in principle and then rounded once, which is fine in isolation, but when three or more numbers are summed the rounding happens at every intermediate step, and the magnitude of the error introduced depends on the magnitude of the intermediate sum. That dependence is what destroys associativity. Consider adding 1.0, then a tiny value like 10⁻²⁰, then −1.0. If the tiny value is added to 1.0 first, it is entirely lost, because the exact sum requires more significant bits than the format provides, so the result rounds back to 1.0 and the final answer is zero. If instead −1.0 is added to 1.0 first, the result is exactly zero, and adding the tiny value preserves it, giving 10⁻²⁰. Both sequences are legitimate evaluations of the same mathematical expression, yet they disagree completely in relative terms. The general principle is that catastrophic cancellation, absorption of small terms by large ones, and the gradual accumulation of half-unit-in-the-last-place errors all depend on the order in which partial sums are formed. Hardware makes no difference to this; it is a property of finite precision, though features like fused multiply-add, extended-precision accumulators, and SIMD lanes with their own partial sums add further variation in where rounding occurs.

Matrix multiplication is essentially a large collection of dot products, each a sum of many products, so it inherits this sensitivity directly. A high-performance implementation almost never sums a dot product strictly left to right. It tiles the computation to fit caches, splits the reduction dimension across vector lanes so that eight or sixteen independent partial sums are maintained and combined at the end, unrolls loops to hide latency with multiple accumulators, and on a GPU may split the reduction across many threads or blocks whose contributions are combined by atomics or a tree reduction in whatever order they happen to finish. Each of these choices corresponds to a different parenthesization of the same sum. Consequently the same matrices multiplied by the same library can yield bitwise different results when the number of threads changes, when a different tile size or kernel is selected for a different matrix shape, when the code runs on hardware with a different vector width, or when nondeterministic atomic ordering is involved. The differences are usually tiny relative to the result, but they are amplified by ill-conditioned problems and by long iterative computations, which is why training runs, numerical solvers, and test suites that demand exact reproducibility must pin thread counts, kernel choices, and reduction strategies, or adopt deterministic or compensated summation at some cost in speed.

Floating-point numbers represent only a finite subset of the reals: a sign, a fixed number of significand bits, and an exponent. When two such numbers are added, the exact mathematical sum usually cannot be represented, so the hardware rounds the result to the nearest representable value. That rounding step is where associativity breaks down. Addition itself is exact in principle; it is the mandatory rounding after each operation that depends on the magnitudes of the operands, and therefore on the order in which they are combined. The classic illustration is adding a large number, its negation, and a small number. If the small value is absorbed into the large one first, its bits fall off the end of the significand and vanish, leaving zero after the cancellation; if the two large values are cancelled first, the small value survives intact. Both results are correctly rounded for the operations actually performed, yet they differ, sometimes catastrophically in relative terms.

Matrix multiplication is built entirely from long summations. Each output element is a dot product of length K, and the accumulation order of those K products is an implementation choice, not part of the mathematical definition. High-performance kernels reorder aggressively: they tile the computation to fit cache and register blocks, unroll loops so several partial accumulators run in parallel across SIMD lanes, use fused multiply-add so that some products are never separately rounded, split the K dimension across threads or GPU blocks and combine partial sums in a tree, and sometimes accumulate through atomics whose arrival order varies from run to run. Every one of these choices produces a different sequence of roundings, so results agree only to within an error bound of roughly the machine epsilon times the sum of absolute products times a factor depending on reduction depth—not bit for bit.

The practical consequence is that the same matrices multiplied by the same library on the same machine can give different low-order bits when the thread count, tile size, batch shape, or hardware generation changes, and different libraries or precisions diverge more. On well-conditioned data the discrepancies are tiny and harmless, but they are not always harmless. In iterative solvers, eigenvalue routines, or optimization loops, a difference of one bit can flip a comparison, change a pivot choice, alter convergence after a different number of steps, and eventually produce visibly different output. In machine learning, two training runs seeded identically can drift apart for the same reason, complicating debugging and regression testing.

Remedies exist but cost performance: fixing a canonical reduction order, disabling atomic or split-K accumulation, using wider or compensated accumulators, or employing reproducible summation schemes that pre-scale into exactly representable bins so the answer is independent of order.

Floating-point numbers represent only a finite subset of the reals: each value has a fixed number of significand bits, and every arithmetic operation returns the correctly rounded version of the exact mathematical result. Addition itself is exact in intent but not in storage, so whenever the true sum of two numbers needs more significand bits than the format provides, the result is nudged to the nearest representable value. That rounding step is where associativity dies. Consider adding 1.0, then a tiny value like 2⁻⁶⁰, then −1.0 in double precision. Adding 1.0 and 2⁻⁶⁰ first gives exactly 1.0 again, because the small quantity falls entirely below the last bit of the significand, so the final result is zero. Grouping the other way, the tiny value survives and the answer is 2⁻⁶⁰. Both computations are individually correct to within a rounding error, yet they disagree completely in relative terms. More generally, the error of a summation depends on the magnitudes of the intermediate partial sums, so any reordering or regrouping changes which absorptions and cancellations occur. Subtraction of nearby quantities amplifies the effect, since cancellation strips away leading digits and promotes previously negligible rounding noise into the leading digits of the answer.

Matrix multiplication is nothing but a large collection of dot products, each of which is a summation over the contracted dimension. High-performance implementations never evaluate those sums left to right. They tile the problem to fit caches and registers, split the contraction dimension across threads, warps, or entire devices, accumulate partial results in vector lanes that are combined pairwise at the end, and often use fused multiply-add so that the product is not rounded before being added. The particular grouping chosen depends on the tile sizes, the number of threads, the hardware's vector width, whether split-k or atomic accumulation is used, and which of several kernels an autotuner selects for a given shape. Every one of those choices is a different parenthesization of the same mathematical sum, and therefore generally yields a slightly different floating-point answer.

The practical consequence is that the "same" matrix multiplication can give bitwise different results on a different GPU, a different library version, a different batch size, or even between two runs on the same machine if atomics complete in a nondeterministic order. Individually the discrepancies are near the unit roundoff, but they compound through deep networks, iterative solvers, and long simulations, breaking bitwise reproducibility, complicating regression testing and debugging, and occasionally flipping decisions that depend on comparisons. Remedies include fixing the reduction order in deterministic kernels, accumulating in wider precision, or using compensated or exactly-rounded summation, each trading some throughput for repeatability.

Floating-point numbers occupy a finite set of values, so almost every arithmetic operation must round its exact result to the nearest representable neighbor. IEEE 754 addition is correctly rounded, meaning each individual sum is as accurate as the format allows, but rounding is applied after every operation, and the amount of information discarded depends on the magnitudes of the operands involved. Because different groupings present the hardware with different intermediate magnitudes, they discard different bits. A standard illustration in double precision: adding ten quadrillion, one, and negative ten quadrillion left to right gives zero, because the one is absorbed entirely by the large value and then cancelled away, while adding the last two first gives exactly one. Addition remains commutative, but associativity fails, and so does distributivity of multiplication over addition. Cancellation, absorption of small addends into large accumulators, and order-dependent overflow or underflow are all manifestations of the same finite-precision truncation.

Matrix multiplication is a dense collection of dot products, and a dot product is a reduction whose order is essentially unconstrained by the mathematics but heavily constrained by performance. High-performance implementations therefore reorder freely: they block the contraction dimension for cache and register reuse, keep several independent SIMD accumulators in flight to hide floating-point latency, use fused multiply-add so that a product is accumulated without an intermediate rounding, split the reduction across threads or GPU blocks and combine partial sums in a tree or through atomic updates, and select among many tuned kernels based on matrix shape, alignment, core count, and hardware generation. Every one of these choices fixes a particular association of the sum, and each association carries its own rounding error. Sequential accumulation has a worst-case error growing roughly linearly in the contraction length, while pairwise or blocked accumulation grows roughly logarithmically, so results are not merely different but differently accurate.

The practical consequence is that bitwise identical output cannot be assumed across machines, thread counts, library versions, or even successive runs when atomics introduce nondeterministic combination order. The per-element discrepancies are usually near the rounding-error level, which is harmless for well-conditioned downstream use, but they are not always harmless. Comparisons, argmax and tie-breaking, thresholding, convergence tests in iterative solvers, and long training loops can amplify a last-bit difference into visibly divergent behavior, which frustrates debugging, regression testing, and certification. Remedies exist and all cost something: pinning a deterministic kernel and thread count, accumulating in wider precision, using compensated summation, or employing reproducible schemes based on exact long accumulators or pre-rounding, which guarantee an order-independent result at some loss of throughput.

Floating-point numbers occupy a finite number of bits, so most real values cannot be stored exactly. A typical double-precision number carries 53 bits of significand, and every arithmetic operation must round its ideal mathematical result back into that format. Addition is where this rounding bites hardest, because adding numbers of very different magnitudes requires aligning their exponents, which shifts the smaller operand's significand to the right and pushes its least significant bits past the end of the available field. Those bits are discarded, and the discarded amount depends on which operands happen to meet each other. Consider a large value, a small value, and the negation of the large value. Adding the two large-magnitude terms first yields exactly zero, and the small value survives intact. Adding the large value to the small one first rounds the small contribution away entirely, so the subsequent cancellation leaves nothing. The two groupings differ by the whole of the small term. Each individual addition is correctly rounded and the hardware is behaving exactly as specified; it is associativity itself that fails, because rounding is not a linear operation and the error committed at each step depends on the running partial sum.

Matrix multiplication is built almost entirely out of long summations: each output entry is a dot product over the shared dimension. Mathematically the order of that summation is irrelevant, so any implementation is free to choose whichever order best exploits the machine. High-performance libraries exploit this freedom aggressively. They tile the computation to fit caches, split the reduction dimension across threads or GPU blocks and combine partial sums in a tree, use vector registers so that lanes accumulate independent interleaved subsequences, apply fused multiply-add so that some products are never rounded at all, and occasionally invoke Strassen-like schemes that replace additions of products with products of sums. Every one of these choices fixes a different grouping of the same terms, and therefore a different pattern of rounding error.

The consequence is that the same mathematical product, computed on a different number of threads, on a different GPU with a different number of streaming multiprocessors, after a library update that retunes tile sizes, or simply with a different alignment of the input arrays that changes the vectorized prologue, can yield results that differ in the last few bits. Those differences are individually tiny but not harmless: they propagate through iterative solvers, training loops, and branch conditions, so two runs can diverge visibly over time. Bitwise reproducibility therefore requires deliberately pinning the reduction order, for instance by using deterministic kernels, fixed thread counts, or compensated and higher-precision accumulation, usually at some cost in speed.

Floating-point numbers occupy a finite number of bits, so each value is drawn from a discrete set with limited precision — in IEEE 754 double precision, roughly sixteen significant decimal digits. When two such numbers are added, the exact mathematical sum generally requires more significant digits than the format can hold, so the hardware rounds the result to the nearest representable value. That rounding step is where associativity breaks down: the intermediate value that gets rounded depends on which pair of operands you combine first, and once information is discarded by rounding it cannot be recovered by later additions. The classic illustration is adding a large number, its negation, and a tiny number. Grouped one way, the large quantities cancel exactly and the tiny value survives; grouped the other way, the tiny value is swallowed entirely by the large one because their exponents differ by more than the width of the significand, and the final answer is zero. Both results are correctly rounded for the operations actually performed, yet they differ. Cancellation makes this worse, because subtracting nearly equal quantities amplifies the relative weight of whatever rounding error was already present.

Matrix multiplication is essentially a vast collection of dot products, and each dot product is a summation whose order is an implementation choice rather than a mathematical property. A naive loop accumulates strictly left to right. A blocked, cache-aware kernel accumulates partial sums per tile and then combines the tiles. A vectorized kernel keeps several independent accumulators in SIMD lanes and folds them together at the end. A multithreaded implementation splits the reduction dimension across cores and sums the per-core contributions in whatever order they finish. A GPU implementation uses tree reductions across threads within a warp and across blocks, sometimes with atomic accumulation whose ordering depends on scheduling. Every one of these produces a different grouping of the same additions, hence potentially a different final bit pattern. Fused multiply-add instructions add another wrinkle, since they round once rather than twice and thus give results that differ from separate multiply and add even for identical orderings. Mixed-precision hardware that accumulates in a wider format inside the multiply-accumulate unit changes the answer again.

The practical consequence is that the same matrices multiplied by the same library can give different results on different hardware, with different thread counts, with different tile sizes chosen by autotuning, or even between runs when atomics or dynamic work stealing are involved. The discrepancies are usually tiny, but they can be magnified by ill-conditioned problems, iterative solvers, or comparisons against thresholds, which is why deterministic modes, fixed reduction trees, compensated summation, or higher-precision accumulation are offered when bitwise reproducibility genuinely matters.

Floating-point numbers represent only a finite subset of the reals: each value is a sign, a bounded exponent, and a fixed-width significand, typically 24 bits for single precision or 53 for double. When two such numbers are added, the exact mathematical sum often requires more significand bits than the format provides, so the hardware rounds the result to the nearest representable value. That rounding is the source of non-associativity. Consider adding 1.0, then a tiny quantity like 2⁻⁵³, then another 2⁻⁵³ in double precision. Adding the two tiny values first gives 2⁻⁵², which is exactly the spacing of numbers just above 1.0, so the total becomes distinguishably larger than 1.0. Adding 1.0 to one tiny value first rounds back to 1.0, and the second addition rounds away too, leaving 1.0 exactly. The same three operands, grouped differently, give different answers. More dramatic cases arise with catastrophic cancellation, where a large positive and large negative value nearly annihilate: whether the cancellation happens before or after small terms are accumulated can change the relative error by many orders of magnitude, and with extreme exponent ranges one order may overflow to infinity or underflow to zero while another does not. Each individual operation is correctly rounded and deterministic; it is the composition of roundings that depends on order.

This matters for matrix multiplication because every output element is a sum of many products, and high-performance implementations are free to compute that sum in whatever order best exploits the machine. Vectorized kernels maintain several partial accumulators, one per SIMD lane, and combine them at the end, which is a tree reduction rather than a sequential one. Cache-blocked and tiled algorithms split the inner dimension into panels, accumulating partial results that are later added together. Multithreaded and distributed implementations partition the reduction across cores or nodes and merge with an order that can depend on scheduling or network arrival times. GPUs add warp-level shuffles, atomics, and split-K strategies whose grouping varies with launch configuration. Some kernels use fused multiply-add, which rounds once instead of twice, while others do not; some accumulate in wider precision or use Tensor-Core-style mixed-precision paths with their own internal accumulation width.

The consequence is that mathematically identical matrix products can differ in their last bits, and those differences are amplified by ill-conditioned data or by long iterative pipelines such as training loops, where a one-bit divergence can grow into visibly different results. Simply changing thread count, tile size, library version, or hardware generation can perturb output, and non-deterministic atomics can make even repeated runs on one machine disagree. Reproducibility therefore requires deliberately fixing the reduction order, or using order-independent techniques such as compensated or exactly-rounded summation.

Floating-point numbers occupy a finite set of values, and every arithmetic operation must round its exact mathematical result back onto that set. IEEE 754 guarantees that each individual addition is correctly rounded, but rounding is a nonlinear step whose error depends on the magnitudes of the operands involved. Consequently, when three numbers are summed, the intermediate value that gets rounded differs depending on grouping, and so does the final answer. The canonical illustration is adding a very large number, a tiny number, and the negation of the large number: grouping the two large terms first cancels them exactly and preserves the tiny term, whereas adding the large and tiny terms first causes the small one to be absorbed entirely, since the exact sum is not representable and rounds back to the large value. The tiny contribution is destroyed and cannot be recovered. Similar effects arise from catastrophic cancellation, where subtracting nearly equal quantities magnifies the relative weight of earlier rounding errors. Addition remains commutative, since swapping operands does not change the exact sum being rounded, but it is definitively not associative, and therefore not distributive over long sums either.

Matrix multiplication is built almost entirely from such long sums: each output element is a dot product over the contraction dimension. Mathematically the order of accumulation is irrelevant, but computationally it is chosen by the implementation to maximize performance. A high-performance kernel tiles the contraction dimension to fit cache and register blocks, splits it across SIMD lanes so that each lane holds a partial sum later combined in a tree, uses multiple accumulators to hide instruction latency, may fuse multiplies and adds so that one rounding step disappears, and on GPUs may split the reduction across thread blocks whose partial results are combined by atomics in whatever order they happen to finish. Every one of these choices defines a different parenthesization of the same sum, and hence a different pattern of rounding errors. Change the number of threads, the tile size, the library version, the CPU's vector width, or move from CPU to GPU, and the results differ in the last bits even though every operation was correctly rounded and no code is buggy. Nondeterministic atomic ordering makes results differ between runs on the same machine.

These discrepancies are usually tiny per element, bounded roughly by the accumulation length times the machine epsilon times the sum of magnitudes, and tree-shaped reductions actually reduce the bound to logarithmic growth. The practical problem is amplification: ill-conditioned solves, iterative algorithms that branch on comparisons, and deep neural networks can turn last-bit differences into visibly divergent trajectories, which breaks exact-match testing, complicates debugging, and motivates deterministic kernels, fixed reduction orders, wider or compensated accumulators, and reproducible BLAS implementations.

Floating-point numbers are a finite subset of the reals: a binary64 value carries a 53-bit significand and an exponent, so most sums of two representable numbers are not themselves representable and must be rounded to the nearest available value. Each addition therefore introduces a small relative error, bounded by the unit roundoff (about 1.1e-16 for double precision), and crucially the size of that error depends on the magnitudes of the operands involved. Because different groupings pair different magnitudes, the errors differ. A familiar illustration is that (1e16 + 1) − 1e16 evaluates to zero, since adding one to 1e16 falls below the spacing between adjacent representable numbers and is absorbed, while 1e16 + (1 − 1e16) yields one exactly. More extreme discrepancies arise when intermediate partial sums overflow to infinity in one order but stay finite in another, or when they drift into the subnormal range where relative precision degrades. Addition remains commutative, and each individual operation is deterministic and correctly rounded, but the composition of many roundings is order-dependent, so associativity fails.

Matrix multiplication is essentially a huge collection of dot products, and every dot product is a reduction over the contraction dimension. High-performance implementations never sum left to right. They tile the computation to fit cache and register blocks, keep several independent accumulators to hide instruction latency, use SIMD lanes that accumulate partial sums separately before a final horizontal combine, fuse multiply and add so that a product is not rounded before accumulation, and on GPUs split the contraction dimension across many thread blocks whose partial results are merged by a tree or by atomic additions. Every one of these choices fixes a particular summation order. Change the tile size, the number of threads, the batch size, the library version, the vendor, the precision of the accumulator, or whether a split-K path is selected by a heuristic, and the order changes with it. Atomic merges and dynamically scheduled work make the order vary even between two runs of the same binary on the same machine.

The consequence is that the same mathematical product computed two ways agrees only to within roundoff, typically a relative difference on the order of the square root of the contraction length times the unit roundoff, not bit for bit. Such differences are harmless for well-conditioned numerical purposes, but they destroy bitwise reproducibility, and downstream discrete decisions can amplify them without bound: an argmax that flips, a comparison against a threshold, a convergence test that triggers one iteration earlier, or a long training run whose trajectory diverges. Recovering reproducibility requires deliberately constraining the reduction, through deterministic kernels with a fixed order, compensated or extended-precision accumulation, or exact summation with wide accumulators, each of which trades throughput for repeatability, and none of which by itself guarantees greater accuracy.

Floating-point numbers are stored with a fixed number of significand bits, so most arithmetic results cannot be represented exactly and must be rounded to the nearest representable value. Each individual addition in IEEE-754 is correctly rounded, meaning it produces the exactly rounded result of the true sum of its two operands, but that rounding is a lossy operation, and the amount of information lost depends on the relative magnitudes of the operands. When a large number is added to a very small one, the small number's low-order bits fall off the end of the significand and vanish; when two nearly equal numbers of opposite sign are subtracted, leading bits cancel and the remaining low-order bits, already contaminated by earlier rounding, are promoted to significance. Because the loss depends on the operands, the order in which a chain of additions is performed changes which bits get discarded. A classic illustration: in double precision, adding 1 to 10^20 returns 10^20 unchanged, so (10^20 + 1) − 10^20 evaluates to zero while 10^20 + (1 − 10^20) evaluates to one. Both computations follow the standard faithfully; the standard simply does not promise associativity, only per-operation correct rounding. Overflow, underflow, and gradual loss into subnormals add further order dependence.

Matrix multiplication is a dense collection of dot products, and a dot product is exactly such a chain of additions. Nothing in the mathematics fixes the summation order, so implementations choose whatever order is fastest. A cache-blocked kernel accumulates partial sums per tile and combines them later; a vectorized kernel keeps several independent accumulators in SIMD lanes and merges them at the end; a GPU kernel splits the reduction across threads and warps and combines results with a tree, sometimes with atomic additions whose arrival order varies from run to run; a multithreaded CPU kernel may split the k dimension across cores. Each strategy imposes a different parenthesization, and therefore a different rounding trajectory, so the results differ in the last few bits. Fused multiply-add, which rounds once instead of twice, and extended-precision accumulators change results as well, in the direction of greater accuracy but not of agreement.

The practical consequence is that the same matrices multiplied by the same library on different hardware, with a different number of threads, with a different tile size chosen by autotuning, or after a library update, can produce numerically different answers. The differences are usually tiny relative to the result's magnitude, but they can be amplified by ill-conditioned downstream steps, by comparisons and branches, or by long iterative processes such as training a neural network, where a one-bit divergence in the first step grows into visibly different trajectories. Achieving bitwise reproducibility therefore requires deliberately fixing the reduction order, using deterministic kernels, or employing compensated or exact summation techniques, each of which costs performance.

Consequently (a + b) + c and a + (b + c) can differ, because the intermediate value that gets rounded is different in each grouping. The classic illustration uses a large number and two small ones: if a is enormous compared with b and c, then a + b may round straight back to a, and adding c again returns a, so the small contributions vanish entirely; whereas b + c first accumulates the small quantities into something big enough to survive the final rounding. Matrix multiplication is built entirely from sums of products: each output element is a dot product over the shared dimension. Nothing in the mathematics fixes the order in which those products are accumulated, so implementations are free to choose whatever order gives the best performance. The canonical illustration in double precision is that (10^16 + 1) − 10^16 evaluates to zero, because adding one to 10^16 rounds back to 10^16, whereas 10^16 + (1 − 10^16) yields exactly one. More generally, adding a small quantity to a large accumulator can discard it entirely, while summing small quantities together first preserves their contribution. Catastrophic cancellation makes matters worse: when two nearly equal numbers are subtracted, previously harmless rounding errors in their low-order bits become the dominant part of the result. Overflow to infinity, underflow to subnormals, and the use of fused multiply-add, which rounds once instead of twice, add further order sensitivity.

Matrix multiplication is essentially a large collection of dot products, each a reduction over the contraction dimension, and high-performance implementations reorder those reductions aggressively. Blocking for cache, register tiling, and vectorization mean that a length-K dot product is computed as many independent partial sums, one per SIMD lane or accumulator register, later combined in some tree order. Multithreaded and GPU kernels may split the contraction dimension across cores or blocks and combine partial results with atomics, so the arrival order varies between runs even on identical hardware. Different libraries, different tile sizes chosen by autotuning, different thread counts, and different accumulator precisions in tensor-core paths all produce different groupings. Every such grouping is a legitimate answer, yet they differ in the low-order bits.

The magnitude of the discrepancy is bounded roughly by the machine epsilon times the number of terms times the sum of absolute products for naive sequential summation, and by something like the logarithm of the length for tree-shaped reductions, so blocked parallel schemes are often more accurate as well as faster. Still, the results are not bitwise identical, and that matters whenever downstream logic amplifies small differences: iterative solvers may take different numbers of iterations, pivot selection or comparison-based branches may flip, ill-conditioned or chaotic computations may diverge visibly, and neural network training runs become unrepeatable, complicating debugging and regression testing. Remedies include pinning thread counts and library versions, using deterministic kernels with a fixed reduction order, accumulating in higher precision, or employing compensated summation and exact long accumulators to make the result independent of order.

# Why Floating-Point Addition Is Not Associative

Floating-point numbers represent reals with a fixed number of significand bits — 24 for single precision, 53 for double. Every arithmetic operation produces an exact mathematical result that is then rounded to the nearest representable value. This rounding is where associativity dies. Consider adding 1.0, 2⁻⁵³, and 2⁻⁵³ in double precision. If you compute (1.0 + 2⁻⁵³) + 2⁻⁵³, the first sum needs 54 bits of significand and rounds back to exactly 1.0, and the second addition does the same, so the answer is 1.0. If instead you compute 1.0 + (2⁻⁵³ + 2⁻⁵³), the inner sum is exactly 2⁻⁵², which is representable and large enough to move the last bit of 1.0, giving a result strictly greater than 1.0. Same three numbers, different grouping, different answer. The general mechanism is that adding a small quantity to a large one discards low-order bits; whether those bits survive long enough to accumulate depends entirely on the order in which partial sums are formed. Catastrophic cancellation compounds this, since a subtraction of nearly equal quantities can promote tiny rounding errors into the leading digits of the result.

Matrix multiplication is nothing but a large collection of dot products, and each dot product is a reduction — a sum of many products whose grouping is unspecified by the mathematics. High-performance implementations aggressively restructure these reductions. A vectorized kernel keeps several independent accumulators, one per SIMD lane, and combines them only at the end. Cache blocking splits the summation over k into tiles that are accumulated separately. Multithreaded and GPU implementations partition k across threads or warps and combine partial results through tree reductions or atomics whose interleaving may not even be deterministic between runs. Fused multiply-add instructions change matters further by rounding once instead of twice. Every one of these choices is a different parenthesization of the same mathematical sum, so every one may yield a slightly different floating-point result.

The practical consequence is that the "same" matrix multiplication gives bitwise different answers when the tile size changes, when the thread count changes, when the library dispatches to a different kernel because the matrix dimensions crossed a heuristic threshold, or when the code moves to hardware with different vector widths. Individually the discrepancies sit near machine epsilon, but iterative algorithms, deep neural networks, and long simulations amplify them, so two runs can diverge visibly and regression tests based on exact comparison become meaningless. Reproducibility therefore requires deliberate effort: fixing the reduction order, using deterministic library modes, or employing compensated or exactly-rounded summation, all of which trade performance for bitwise stability.

A classic illustration in double precision: adding 1 to 10^16 leaves 10^16 unchanged, because the gap between neighboring doubles there exceeds 1, so (10^16 + 1) − 10^16 evaluates to zero, while 10^16 + (1 − 10^16) evaluates to 1. Small quantities are absorbed when combined with large ones, and cancellation can later expose the loss; whether that happens depends entirely on grouping. Similar effects arise with subnormals, with overflow to infinity in one ordering but not another, and with fused multiply-add, which rounds once instead of twice and therefore also perturbs results relative to separate multiply and add.

Matrix multiplication is essentially a large collection of dot products, each a reduction over K terms, so it inherits this sensitivity directly. High-performance implementations never sum in the naive left-to-right order. They tile the computation for cache and register reuse, so partial sums accumulate per block and are combined afterward; they vectorize, so a SIMD register holds several independent partial accumulators that are only merged at the end; they may split the K dimension across threads or GPU blocks and combine partial results through a tree reduction, atomic additions, or a second kernel pass; and they may use FMA in some code paths but not others. Every one of these choices fixes a different parenthesization of the same mathematical sum, and each parenthesization can round differently. Consequently the same matrices multiplied by the same library can yield bitwise different answers when the thread count changes, when the tile size or kernel is selected differently because of matrix shape or alignment, when atomics complete in a different nondeterministic order, or when the code runs on a different microarchitecture or accelerator.

The individual discrepancies are tiny, bounded roughly by machine epsilon times the sum of absolute values of the products, but they are not harmless. Exact-equality tests fail, ill-conditioned problems magnify the difference, and iterative processes such as neural network training, eigensolvers, or simulations can amplify a last-bit divergence into visibly different trajectories after many steps. Reproducibility therefore requires deliberately pinning the reduction order, using deterministic kernels, or accumulating in higher precision or with compensated summation or fixed-point accumulators, all of which trade some speed or parallel flexibility for bitwise repeatability.

When two such numbers are added, the exact mathematical sum often needs more significand bits than the format provides, so the hardware rounds the result to the nearest representable value. The classic illustration is adding a huge number, its negation, and a tiny number. If you first add the huge number to the tiny one, the tiny one is shifted so far right that it falls entirely off the end of the significand and is absorbed; the result is the huge number unchanged, and subtracting the huge number leaves zero. If instead you first cancel the two large values exactly, you are left with the tiny number intact. Both orders are legitimate evaluations of the same expression, yet they differ by the entire magnitude of the small term. More generally, whenever operands vary widely in magnitude or whenever cancellation occurs, the accumulated rounding error depends strongly on the sequence in which partial sums are formed; summing many similar-magnitude values sequentially tends to be worse than pairwise or blocked summation, because the running total grows large relative to each new addend and low-order bits are repeatedly discarded.

Matrix multiplication is essentially a vast collection of dot products, each of which is a reduction over the shared dimension, so it inherits this sensitivity directly. Consequently the same mathematical product can yield results differing in the last few bits, and those differences can amplify through subsequent iterations, ill-conditioned solves, or comparisons against thresholds, so training runs or simulations diverge visibly. Associativity fails because the rounding error introduced at each step depends on the *magnitudes* of the intermediate operands, and regrouping changes those intermediates. A standard illustration in double precision: 10^16 + 1 rounds back to 10^16, since the exact answer needs more than 53 significand bits, so (10^16 + 1) − 10^16 evaluates to 0, whereas 10^16 + (1 − 10^16) evaluates to 1. The same phenomenon appears in milder forms everywhere: small addends are partially absorbed by large accumulators, and cancellation between nearly equal terms exposes rounding noise that was previously hidden in low-order bits. The result is that a sum of many numbers has no single "correct" floating-point value, only a family of values within an error bound that grows roughly linearly with the number of terms for sequential accumulation and logarithmically for balanced pairwise or tree summation.

Matrix multiplication is essentially a large collection of such reductions: every output entry is a dot product of length K. High-performance implementations never compute those dot products in naive left-to-right order. They block and tile for cache reuse, keep several independent SIMD accumulators in flight to hide instruction latency, fuse multiply and add so that a product is rounded once rather than twice, split the K dimension across threads or GPU blocks and combine partial sums in whatever order those partials happen to finish, and sometimes accumulate in a different precision than the inputs, as tensor-core and mixed-precision paths do. Each of these choices defines a different summation tree over the same K products. Consequently the same mathematical product computed on a CPU and a GPU, with two thread counts, with two library versions, with a different tile size chosen by autotuning, or with atomic accumulation whose order varies run to run, can yield results that differ in the last few bits of the mantissa.

Those differences are individually negligible relative to the magnitude of the entries, but they are not harmless. Ill-conditioned matrices amplify them; iterative processes such as training loops, eigensolvers, or long simulations compound them; and any discrete decision layered on top, such as an argmax, a sort, a comparison against a tolerance, or a convergence test, can convert a one-bit discrepancy into a visibly different outcome. Achieving bitwise reproducibility therefore requires deliberately fixing the reduction order, or using compensated summation, wider accumulators, or exact fixed-point superaccumulators, each of which trades some throughput or flexibility for determinism.

Floating-point numbers represent only a finite subset of the reals, so every arithmetic operation must round its exact result to the nearest representable value. Addition is therefore not exact but rather "add, then round," and because the rounding error depends on the magnitudes of the operands, the errors introduced by a sequence of additions depend on the order in which those additions are performed. A classic illustration: if you add a very large number to a very small one, the small one can be absorbed entirely, contributing nothing, whereas if you first accumulate many small numbers together they may grow large enough to affect the final sum. Thus (a + b) + c and a + (b + c) can differ, sometimes drastically when cancellation between large nearly-equal quantities exposes low-order bits that were already lost. Addition remains commutative — swapping two operands of a single addition changes nothing — but it is not associative, and this is a property of the IEEE 754 model itself, not a defect of any particular processor.

Matrix multiplication is essentially a large collection of dot products, each of which is a reduction over the contraction dimension. Mathematically the sum is order-independent, but numerically it is not, and high-performance implementations aggressively reorder it. Vectorized kernels keep several partial sums in separate SIMD lanes and combine them at the end, effectively performing a strided or tree-shaped reduction. Cache blocking splits the contraction dimension into panels whose partial results are accumulated separately. Multithreaded and GPU kernels may split the reduction across cores or blocks, with the number of splits chosen by heuristics that depend on matrix shape, available parallelism, or autotuning. Fused multiply-add rounds once instead of twice, and some kernels accumulate in wider precision than the inputs. Algorithms like Strassen's replace sums outright. Consequently the same mathematical product, computed by two libraries, two hardware generations, two thread counts, or even two runs of a kernel that uses atomics or nondeterministic work scheduling, can yield results differing in the last few bits.

The magnitude of these discrepancies is usually bounded by roughly the condition number of the sum times the accumulated rounding error, which grows about linearly with the contraction length for naive sequential accumulation and only logarithmically for tree reductions, so the differences are typically tiny. They matter, though, because downstream computations can amplify them: iterative solvers may take different numbers of iterations, comparisons and branches may flip, ill-conditioned problems may diverge, and machine-learning training runs may separate over time. Achieving bit-identical results therefore requires deliberately fixing the reduction order, or using order-independent techniques such as compensated summation, wider accumulators, or exact fixed-point accumulation, generally at some cost in speed.

Floating-point numbers occupy a finite set of values, and every arithmetic operation must round its exact mathematical result to the nearest representable member of that set. Addition itself is commutative — the order of the two operands does not matter — but the rounding step destroys associativity, because the intermediate value that gets rounded depends on how the operands are grouped. A classic illustration in double precision: if you add 1.0 to 10⁻²⁰, the tiny value falls far below the roughly sixteen significant decimal digits that the format can hold, so the sum rounds back to exactly 1.0 and the small quantity is annihilated. Then subtracting 1.0 yields zero. Group the same three numbers differently, computing 10⁻²⁰ plus the difference of 1.0 and 1.0, and you get 10⁻²⁰ exactly. Both results are individually correct to within one rounding error of their respective intermediate sums, yet they differ enormously in relative terms. More generally, each addition can introduce a relative error on the order of the machine epsilon, and the accumulated error depends on the magnitudes of the partial sums encountered along the way, which is precisely what reordering changes. Cancellation between operands of similar magnitude and opposite sign magnifies the effect, since it strips away leading digits and promotes previously negligible rounding noise into the significant part of the answer.

Matrix multiplication is a dense collection of dot products, and a dot product is a sum of many products, so it is exactly the situation where grouping matters. On modern hardware there is no single canonical grouping. A naive loop accumulates left to right in one register; a vectorized kernel keeps several partial sums in SIMD lanes and combines them at the end; a cache-blocked implementation splits the reduction dimension into tiles and adds tile contributions in whatever order the scheduler produces; a GPU splits a dot product across threads, warps, and blocks, reducing through shared memory and sometimes through atomics whose arrival order is nondeterministic from run to run. Fused multiply–add, which rounds once instead of twice, changes results again, as do extended-precision or Kahan-compensated accumulators and mixed-precision tensor units that accumulate in a wider format than they multiply in.

The practical consequence is that the same mathematical product computed by two libraries, or by one library on two different thread counts, tile sizes, or hardware generations, will generally agree only to within accumulated rounding error rather than bit for bit. Usually this is harmless, but in iterative solvers, chaotic dynamics, or training runs where tiny differences are amplified over many steps, it breaks exact reproducibility. Remedies include fixing the reduction tree regardless of parallel resources, using deterministic kernels, or employing exact or compensated summation, all of which trade some performance for bitwise repeatability.

The identity (a+b)+c = a+(b+c) therefore holds only in exact arithmetic, which hardware does not implement.

Matrix multiplication is a vast collection of dot products, and a dot product is a reduction — precisely the operation whose result depends on ordering. Which path executes depends on matrix shape, thread count, library version, autotuning heuristics, and the specific processor, so the same nominal call can perform the same additions in many different orders.

The consequence is that results agree only to within rounding error, never bit for bit. Discrepancies are typically on the order of the unit roundoff times the accumulated magnitude, growing with the length of the reduction and far worse when terms cancel; when atomics are involved, the order can differ between two runs on the same machine, so results are not even repeatable. No ordering is wrong, so bitwise reproducibility must be purchased deliberately — through fixed reduction trees, deterministic kernels, wider or compensated accumulation, or exact accumulators — and it is usually paid for in performance.

They tile the operands for cache and register reuse, split the inner dimension into blocks handled by different threads or different GPU warps, accumulate into multiple vector lanes that are combined pairwise at the end, and sometimes use fused multiply–add so that the product is not rounded before accumulation. Change the number of threads, the tile size, the vector width, whether a fast path with a different blocking is selected for a particular shape, or the order in which asynchronous partial results arrive at an atomic accumulator, and the reduction tree changes shape. The output then differs in the low-order bits even though the code, the inputs, and the hardware arithmetic are all identical and correct.

Consequently bitwise reproducibility is not a property of the mathematics but of a pinned execution schedule. Small discrepancies compound through iterative solvers, training loops, and branch conditions, so two runs can diverge visibly. Remedies include fixing thread counts and algorithm selection, using deterministic reduction trees, higher-precision or compensated accumulators, or exact fixed-point superaccumulators, each trading speed for repeatability.

Floating-point numbers represent only a finite subset of the reals, and every arithmetic operation must round its exact result to the nearest representable value. Addition itself is commutative, but rounding depends on the magnitudes of the operands, so the order in which sums are accumulated changes where information is discarded. The canonical illustration uses a large value and two small ones: in double precision, (1.0 + 10⁻¹⁶) rounds back to exactly 1.0 because the tiny addend falls below the last bit of the larger number's significand, so ((1.0 + 10⁻¹⁶) + 10⁻¹⁶) yields 1.0, while (1.0 + (10⁻¹⁶ + 10⁻¹⁶)) first forms 2×10⁻¹⁶, which is large enough to survive rounding and shifts the result. Cancellation compounds this: when nearly equal quantities are subtracted, previously harmless rounding errors in the operands become a large relative error in the difference. Consequently the accumulated error of a length-n sum depends on the summation tree, with worst-case bounds growing like n times the machine epsilon for sequential accumulation but only like log n for balanced pairwise trees.

High-performance implementations never sum in the naive left-to-right order. They tile the computation for cache reuse, so a dot product is split into blocks whose partial results are combined later; they vectorize, so a single SIMD register holds several independent partial sums that are merged at the end; they use fused multiply-add, which rounds once instead of twice per term; they parallelize across threads or GPU blocks, sometimes splitting the reduction dimension and combining contributions through atomics whose interleaving varies from run to run; and they may use lower-precision multipliers with wider accumulators, as tensor-core paths do, or fast algorithms such as Strassen's that change the arithmetic entirely.

The result is that two mathematically identical multiplications can differ in their last bits, and the differences are not merely cosmetic. Changing the number of threads, the tile size, the library version, the CPU's vector width, or moving from CPU to GPU can perturb outputs, and atomic-based reductions can make a single machine nondeterministic across repeated runs. Small perturbations then propagate: iterative solvers may take different numbers of iterations or converge to slightly different points, branch decisions on comparisons may flip, and long training runs in machine learning can diverge visibly. Remedies exist but cost performance or generality, including pinning a fixed reduction order, using deterministic kernels, employing compensated summation or extended-precision accumulators, or using reproducible libraries built on exact accumulation techniques that make the answer independent of ordering.

# Why Floating-Point Addition Loses Associativity

Floating-point numbers represent reals with a fixed number of significand bits — 24 for single precision, 53 for double. Every arithmetic operation produces an exact mathematical result that is then rounded to the nearest representable value. This rounding is where associativity dies. Consider adding 1.0, then a tiny value like 2⁻⁵³, then another 2⁻⁵³ in double precision. If you compute (1.0 + 2⁻⁵³) + 2⁻⁵³, the first addition must round, and since 1.0 + 2⁻⁵³ falls exactly halfway to the next representable number, round-to-even returns 1.0; the second addition does the same, yielding 1.0. # Why Floating-Point Addition Loses Associativity

Floating-point numbers represent reals with a fixed number of significant bits — 24 for single precision, 53 for double. Every arithmetic operation must return a result in that same format, so the exact mathematical sum of two representable numbers is generally rounded to the nearest representable neighbour. This rounding is where associativity dies. Consider adding 1.0, then a tiny value like 2⁻⁶⁰, then −1.0 in double precision. Grouping as (1.0 + 2⁻⁶⁰) + (−1.0) gives zero, because 2⁻⁶⁰ is far below the precision available next to 1.0 and is discarded entirely by rounding. Grouping as 1.0 + (2⁻⁶⁰ + (−1.0)) preserves the small quantity, since it is added to a number of comparable magnitude before the cancellation occurs. Both orders are correctly rounded at every step; they simply round at different moments, and the discarded information differs. The general phenomenon is absorption of small addends by large partial sums, compounded by catastrophic cancellation when nearly equal quantities subtract and expose earlier rounding error as a large relative error. Each individual operation is off by at most half an ulp, but the accumulation of those errors depends on the sequence of partial sums, which depends on the grouping.

Nothing in the mathematical definition prescribes the order of that summation, so implementations choose orders that suit the machine. Vectorised code keeps several independent accumulators, one per SIMD lane, and merges them at the end. Multithreaded code partitions by rows, columns, or depth depending on the shape. Fused multiply-add instructions add a further wrinkle by skipping an intermediate rounding, so results differ even for identical orderings. Consequently the same matrices multiplied by the same library can yield bitwise different answers on different hardware, with different thread counts, with different tile sizes chosen by autotuning, or even between two runs when atomics are involved.

The differences are usually tiny in relative terms, bounded roughly by the condition number times machine epsilon times the reduction length, but they are not always harmless. IEEE 754 requires each individual operation to return the exact result rounded to the nearest representable value, which means every addition can introduce a small error whose size depends on the magnitude of the operands involved at that moment. Because the operands differ depending on the order in which sums are formed, the accumulated error differs too. A concrete illustration in double precision: adding 1 to 2^53 gives back 2^53, since 2^53 + 1 falls exactly halfway between neighbouring representable values and rounds to even, so (2^53 + 1) − 2^53 evaluates to zero, whereas 2^53 + (1 − 2^53) evaluates to exactly 1. Addition remains commutative, but it is not associative, and the failure can be arbitrarily large when cancellation exposes bits that an earlier rounding has already discarded. Subnormal flushing, overflow to infinity, and the presence or absence of a fused multiply-add, which skips one rounding of the product, add further order-dependent discrepancies.

Matrix multiplication is a dense collection of dot products, and each dot product is a sum of K terms whose grouping mathematics leaves entirely free but arithmetic does not. Real implementations exploit that freedom aggressively. Cache blocking sums over tiles of the K dimension and combines partial tiles at the end; SIMD code keeps several independent accumulators in vector lanes and merges them with a horizontal reduction; multithreaded and multi-GPU kernels split K across workers and combine partial results, sometimes via atomics whose interleaving varies from run to run; matrix engines and tensor cores accumulate internally in a fixed, sometimes wider, format according to a hardware-defined tree. Every one of these choices is a different association of the same sum, so every one can yield a different rounded answer.

The practical consequence is that a product computed on one thread count, one library version, one GPU model, or even twice on the same machine under dynamic scheduling need not be bit-identical. Typical discrepancies are on the order of the accumulated rounding error, roughly proportional to K times the unit roundoff times the magnitude of the intermediate terms, and they grow when terms nearly cancel or the data are badly scaled. Small bit differences matter when downstream code makes discrete decisions — comparisons, thresholds, pivot selection, argmax over near-ties — or when results feed iterative or chaotic processes that amplify them, which is why long training runs or simulations can visibly diverge. Bitwise reproducibility therefore requires deliberately fixing the reduction order, or using compensated, extended-precision, or exact fixed-point accumulation, all of which cost performance.

# Why Floating-Point Addition Isn't Associative

Floating-point numbers represent real values with a fixed number of significant bits — 24 for single precision, 53 for double. Every arithmetic operation produces an exact mathematical result that must then be rounded to the nearest representable value. This rounding step is where associativity breaks down, because the rounding error depends on the magnitudes of the operands involved, and different groupings expose different magnitudes.

Consider adding 1.0, then a very small value like 10⁻²⁰, then −1.0 in double precision. If you compute (1.0 + 10⁻²⁰) first, the tiny value falls entirely below the trailing bit of 1.0 and vanishes in the rounding; subtracting 1.0 then yields exactly zero. If instead you compute 1.0 + (10⁻²⁰ + (−1.0)), the small value is added to −1.0 and again lost, but the intermediate is −1.0 plus a representable perturbation, and the final result can differ. More dramatically, summing a long sequence of similar-magnitude numbers in order causes the running total to grow while the addends stay small, so each addend loses relative precision; summing them pairwise keeps operands comparable and preserves far more accuracy. Both answers are correct to within the guarantees of the standard, but they are not the same bits.

This has direct consequences for matrix multiplication, where each output element is a dot product — a reduction over the shared dimension. The mathematical definition says nothing about the order in which those products are accumulated, and high-performance implementations exploit that freedom aggressively. A library may tile the reduction dimension into blocks sized to fit cache, accumulate partial sums in vector registers with several independent accumulators to hide instruction latency, and then combine those partial sums at the end. On a GPU, the reduction may be split across many threads, each handling a strip, with results merged through shared memory or atomic operations whose completion order is nondeterministic. The number of threads, the tile sizes, the vector width, and whether fused multiply-add instructions are used all change the effective grouping of additions.

The result is that the same matrix multiply, mathematically identical, can produce different low-order bits when run with a different thread count, on different hardware, with a different library version, or even twice on the same machine if atomics are involved. Individually these discrepancies are tiny, on the order of machine epsilon times the magnitude of the accumulated terms. But they propagate: in iterative solvers, training loops, or chaotic dynamical simulations, small divergences amplify until trajectories separate visibly. Achieving bitwise reproducibility therefore requires deliberately fixing the reduction order, or using compensated and exact summation techniques, at some cost in performance.

# Why Floating-Point Addition Is Not Associative

Floating-point numbers represent real values with finite precision: a sign, a fixed-width significand, and an exponent. Because the significand has only a limited number of bits — 24 for single precision, 53 for double — most arithmetic results cannot be stored exactly and must be rounded to the nearest representable value. Rounding is what destroys associativity. When you compute (a + b) + c, the intermediate sum a + b is rounded before c is added, and that rounding error is then carried into the second operation. Computing a + (b + c) rounds a different intermediate quantity, so the two expressions can differ in their final bits, and occasionally by far more than a few bits.

But a + (b + c) first adds c to b, where c is so small relative to b that it is absorbed entirely by rounding; the result is just b, and adding a gives zero. The tiny quantity has vanished. Catastrophic cancellation of this kind means the error is not merely a matter of trailing digits but can consume the entire significance of the answer. Non-deterministic scheduling, such as atomic accumulation whose order depends on which thread arrives first, makes runs vary even on identical hardware.

The consequence is that the same logical matrix multiplication can produce bitwise different results across library versions, thread counts, tile sizes, or GPU models. Individually these differences sit near the rounding threshold, but in iterative algorithms, chaotic dynamics, or training loops with branching on comparisons, they amplify into visibly divergent trajectories. Matrix multiplication is a dense collection of dot products, and a dot product is a reduction over many terms. Any reduction over more than two elements admits many valid orderings: sequential left-to-right accumulation, pairwise or tree summation, blocked accumulation into several partial sums held in vector lanes, splitting the contraction dimension across threads or blocks that later combine their partials, or atomic accumulation whose arrival order varies from run to run. Achieving bitwise reproducibility therefore requires deliberate constraints: pinning a single kernel and thread count, forcing a fixed reduction tree, using compensated summation or wider accumulators, or employing exact fixed-point accumulation, all of which cost performance.

Matrix multiplication is essentially a large collection of dot products, and a dot product is a sum. On modern hardware, that sum is almost never evaluated in a single fixed order. Vector instructions accumulate several independent partial sums in separate lanes and combine them at the end; compilers unroll loops to hide latency, creating multiple accumulators; cache-blocking splits the reduction dimension into tiles whose partial results are added later; multithreaded and multi-GPU implementations partition the reduction across workers and merge in whatever order they finish. Fused multiply-add instructions further change results by keeping the product at full precision before rounding, and mixed-precision tensor units may accumulate in a wider format than the inputs. Consequently the same logical product of the same matrices can yield bit-different answers when the number of threads changes, when a different tile size or kernel is selected for a different problem shape, when the library dispatches to another instruction set, or simply when atomic updates race in a nondeterministic order.

The differences are typically tiny, near the level of rounding error, but they do not stay tiny. Iterative solvers, optimization loops, and neural network training amplify small discrepancies until trajectories diverge visibly, and comparisons or branches on nearly equal values can flip. Reproducibility therefore has to be engineered: fix the thread count and blocking, use deterministic reduction trees or compensated summation, avoid atomics, or accumulate in higher precision so that ordering differences fall below the reported precision.

Floating-point numbers are stored with a fixed number of significand bits, so most results of an arithmetic operation cannot be represented exactly and must be rounded to the nearest representable value. Addition on IEEE-754 hardware is correctly rounded, meaning it computes the exact sum and then rounds once; the operation itself is faithful, but the rounding is a lossy step that depends on the magnitudes of the two operands. Because the loss depends on what is being added to what, changing the grouping of a sum changes where and how much information is discarded. The classic illustration uses a large value and two tiny ones: if a huge number absorbs a small number, the small contribution vanishes entirely because it falls below the last significand bit of the running total, whereas if the two small numbers are added to each other first they may combine into something large enough to survive. Thus (a + b) + c and a + (b + c) can differ, sometimes dramatically when catastrophic cancellation is involved, even though both are the correctly rounded result of their own grouping. Addition remains commutative — swapping the two operands of a single addition gives an identical result — but it is not associative, and it is not distributive with multiplication either.

Matrix multiplication is a dense collection of dot products, and a dot product is precisely a long chain of additions whose grouping is unconstrained by the mathematical definition. A naive sequential loop accumulates left to right. An optimized implementation almost never does this: it blocks the computation for cache reuse, so partial sums over sub-ranges of the summation index are formed and later combined; it vectorizes, so several independent accumulators run in parallel lanes and are added together at the end; it unrolls to hide floating-point latency, again creating multiple accumulators; it may split the summation index across threads or across GPU blocks, with each contribution merged in whatever order the scheduler happens to produce; and it may use fused multiply-add, which skips an intermediate rounding altogether, or a Strassen-like algorithm, which changes the arithmetic entirely. Each of these choices imposes a different reduction tree, and each tree yields a slightly different rounded answer.

The practical consequence is that the same mathematical product computed on a different core count, a different vector width, a different library version, or a different accelerator can differ in its low-order bits. Atomic accumulation and dynamic work stealing make the order nondeterministic even on identical hardware across runs. Individually these discrepancies are tiny, bounded roughly by the condition number times machine epsilon times the number of terms, but they are amplified by iterative processes: two training runs, two solver iterations, or two branches of a comparison can diverge visibly. Achieving bitwise reproducibility therefore requires deliberately fixing the reduction order, using deterministic kernels, or employing compensated or exactly-rounded summation techniques — each at some cost in performance.

A standard double-precision example makes this concrete. Let u be 2^-53. Then 1 + u rounds back to exactly 1, because 1 + u sits halfway between 1 and the next representable number and round-to-nearest-even prefers 1. So (1 + u) + u is 1, while 1 + (u + u) is 1 + 2^-52, the next representable value above 1. The two groupings differ in the last bit. More dramatically, when large and small quantities are mixed, small terms can be absorbed entirely in one order and survive to cancel a large term in another, so the relative discrepancy can be enormous rather than merely one ulp. Matrix multiplication is built entirely from such sums: every output element is a dot product, a reduction over a long chain of products. High-performance implementations do not evaluate that chain left to right. Those tiny differences are not bugs; each is a legitimate rounding of the same exact value.

The practical consequence is that bitwise reproducibility must be engineered rather than assumed. Small discrepancies can be amplified by ill-conditioned downstream operations, by comparisons and branches, or by iterative processes such as training loops, where divergence compounds over time. Remedies include fixing thread counts and reduction trees, using deterministic library modes, compensated or extended-precision accumulation, or integer-based exact accumulators, all of which trade throughput for repeatability.
